claims.text: The Open/Closed Principle: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
claims.source_hint: glossary entry ocp; standard formulation in software design literature

claims.text: Smells.ShippingVnd takes six parameters including bool express and bool pickUp, checks pickUp first, and five of its return statements choose a value with `express ? ... : ...`; the last is `return 0;`.

ShippingFee is an abstract class with abstract int ForOrder(int totalVnd); StandardShipping (0 from 2,000,000, else 30,000), ExpressShipping (60,000) and PickUpInStore (0) are sealed classes overriding it.
In C#, a non-abstract class deriving from an abstract class that does not override every abstract member fails to compile (CS0534).
claims.source_hint: C# compiler error CS0534; learn.microsoft.com C# abstract keyword

claims.text: At stage-0, SamplesTests.cs has ShippingFeeTests checking StandardShipping at 1,999,999 and 2,000,000 and all three kinds via ForOrder(2_000_000); adding a new subclass requires no edit to these tests to keep them passing.
Code that only calls ForOrder through a ShippingFee variable does not change when a new subclass is added; some code still has to create an instance of the new class.
OCP concerns adding new cases; changing how an existing case behaves (e.g. the standard free-shipping threshold) is still an edit to that case's class and does not violate OCP.
claims.source_hint: outline misconception 1; common reading of OCP

claims.text: An abstract class or interface does not by itself give OCP: if callers check which concrete class they have, each new kind still requires editing those checks.
claims.source_hint: outline misconception 2; follows from the OCP definition

claims.text: Adding a same-day kind to Smells.ShippingVnd means editing the method body (a new flag checked among or ahead of the existing branches); the existing returns next to that edit need re-checking.
